a: A prayer of Moses, the man of God.
p: The only psalm credited to Moses opens the fourth book of the Psalter, right after Psalm 89's cry over David's fallen line.
b: "Man of God" is Moses' title in Deuteronomy 33:1 and Joshua 14:6. Placing a prayer of Moses here looks deliberate. Book III ended with the throne of David in the dust (89:38–51). Book IV answers by going back behind David to Moses, to the wilderness years when Israel had no king and no temple, only the LORD as its home (90:1). Moses appears seven times in Book IV (90:0; 99:6; 103:7; 105:26; 106:16, 23, 32) and only once in the rest of the Psalter (77:20). Gerald Wilson argued that Book IV is the editors' answer to the exile: the LORD reigns even when Judah's king does not.

a: A prayer
p: Only Psalm 92 shifts the verse numbers in this part. In Greek and Latin Bibles these psalms are 89 to 100.
b: This site numbers a psalm's title as verse 0. Hebrew Bibles count the title as verse 1. Where the title shares a verse with the first line (Psalms 90, 98, 100 and 101), the Hebrew and English numbers agree. Psalm 92 has a title of its own, so every Hebrew verse there is one higher: English 92:15 is Hebrew 92:16. Psalms 91, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97 and 99 have no title in the Hebrew at all, though the Greek gives each of them one. In the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate, used in Orthodox service books and older Catholic Bibles, Psalms 90 to 101 are numbered 89 to 100.

a: Moses
p: Jewish tradition gave Moses eleven psalms. Most scholars read the title as a later link to the Moses of Deuteronomy.
b: Traditional view. The Talmud lists Moses among the elders whose words are in the Psalter (Bava Batra 14b–15a). The Midrash on Psalms and Rashi say Moses composed the eleven psalms from 90 to 100, which have no other author named, and Rashi pairs them with the eleven tribes Moses blessed in Deuteronomy 33. Many Christian readers, such as Luther, also took the psalm as Moses' own. Critical view. Most scholars date the psalm later, from its language and its closeness to wisdom writing, and read the title as the editors' way of hearing Moses' voice. They point to its many echoes of Moses' songs: "the God who went into labor with you" (Deuteronomy 32:18), "Change your mind" (Exodus 32:12) and "show his servants pity" (Deuteronomy 32:36).

a: you yourself have been our home
p: Ma'on is a dwelling, even an animal's den. The Greek read a similar word, "refuge."
b: Ma'on is a place to live: God's heavenly dwelling (Deuteronomy 26:15), or a lair for jackals (Jeremiah 9:11). Here God himself is the home of a people that has wandered for generations. The word comes back in 91:9, "You have made the Most High your home," one of several links that bind Psalms 90 and 91 together. Deuteronomy 33:27 uses a related word, "The God of ancient times is a shelter." The Greek and Jerome's Latin from the Greek read "refuge" (katafygē, refugium), as if from ma'oz, a word with one letter different. Jerome's version from the Hebrew has "dwelling" (habitaculum).

a: before you brought the earth and the world to birth
p: The verb is used of a woman writhing in childbirth. The mountains are "born," and God brings the earth to birth.
b: Yulladu, "were born," and vatecholel, "you writhed in labor," are birth words. The same verb appears in the Song of Moses: "the God who went into labor with you" (Deuteronomy 32:18). Job hears God ask who gave birth to the sea and the frost (Job 38:8, 29), and Wisdom says she was "brought forth" before the mountains (Proverbs 8:24–25). The Hebrew vowels make God the one in labor. Read with other vowels, the same letters say "and the earth was brought forth," which the Greek and Jerome's Hebrew version follow. Either way the picture is of a world that once did not exist and was born, while God was already there.

a: from the ages past to the ages to come, you are God
p: Olam is a long stretch of time, far past or far future. The line sets God's timelessness against the shortness of human life.
b: Me'olam ad olam is the phrase of the doxologies that close Books I and IV (41:13; Psalm 106:48), so Book IV is framed by it. The Hebrew word olam does not by itself mean timeless eternity in the philosophers' sense; it means time beyond what anyone can see. But set beside "before the mountains were born," it says that God was before the world and will outlast it. The rest of the psalm measures human life against that: a night watch (90:4), grass (90:5–6), a moan (90:9), seventy years (90:10).

a: You turn a human being back into powder
p: Dakka means something crushed to powder. "Turn back" and "go back" are the same verb, which the Targum heard as "repent."
b: Genesis 3:19 says "to dust you will go back," using afar, dust. Psalm 90 uses a rarer word, dakka, "crushed stuff," which elsewhere describes the crushed in spirit (34:18; Isaiah 57:15). The verb shuv runs through the line twice: God turns humans back, and he says, "Go back." Most readers hear both halves as death, the return to the ground. The Targum and many Jewish interpreters hear the second half as a call to repentance: "Repent, O sons of men." "Children of Adam" points back to the first man and his sentence.

a: For a thousand years, as you see them,
t: A thousand years as a day
p: Second Peter turns this verse around to explain why the Lord's coming seems slow. Jewish and Christian writers built calendars on it.
b: Second Peter answers mockers who ask where Christ's promised coming is: "one day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day" (2 Peter 3:8, a fresh rendering). The psalm's point is the shortness of human life; Peter's is God's patience. Jubilees 4:30 says Adam died seventy years short of a thousand, so he died within the "day" of Genesis 2:17, since a thousand years are one day. The Epistle of Barnabas 15:4 used the verse to teach that the world would last six thousand years, a "day" for each day of creation, followed by a Sabbath, an idea that fed later millennial hopes.
r: 2 Peter 3:8–9; Genesis 2:17; Jubilees 4:29–30; Epistle of Barnabas 15:4; Revelation 20:4

a: like one shift of the night watch
p: Israel divided the night into three watches of about four hours. A sleeper does not even notice one go by.
b: The Old Testament knows three night watches: the beginning (Lamentations 2:19), the middle (Judges 7:19, "at the start of the middle watch") and the morning watch (Exodus 14:24). By New Testament times the Roman count of four watches was used (Mark 6:48; Mark 13:35). For a sleeper a watch passes without notice, which makes it an even smaller unit than "yesterday": a thousand years shrink to a few hours of sleep. The next verse picks up the thought of sleep.

a: You flood them away; they are only a sleep.
p: The Hebrew is unclear. It may mean God sweeps people away like a flood, or that they are a dream that ends.
b: Zeramtam shenah yihyu reads word for word "you flood them, sleep they will be." Zaram elsewhere means rain pouring down (77:17). Some readers take "sleep" as death (13:3; 76:5); others as a dream that fades when the sleeper wakes (73:20). Some scholars redivide the words or change one letter to get "you sow them year by year," which fits the grass that follows. The Greek has something quite different: "their nothings will be years." The Plain keeps the Hebrew and its strangeness: human beings are washed away and are as passing as a night's sleep.

a: In the morning they are like grass that sprouts again.
p: In Israel's hot summer, grass that is green at dawn can be dry by evening. It is the Bible's picture of human frailty.
b: The image returns in 92:7, where the wicked "spring up like grass," and in Psalm 103:15–16. Isaiah's "All flesh is grass" (Isaiah 40:6–8) is quoted in 1 Peter 1:24–25, and James 1:10–11 applies it to the rich. The verb chalaf can mean both "sprout anew" and "pass away," so the line may play on both: the grass that comes up fresh is the grass that will soon be gone.

a: For we are used up by your anger
p: Psalm 90 ties the shortness of life to God's anger at sin. Readers have heard it in different ways.
b: The psalm does not treat death as merely natural. Our days slip away "under your fury" (90:9), and our hidden guilt lies open before God (90:8). Jewish readers, following the Targum's heading ("when the people of Israel sinned in the wilderness"), hear the wilderness generation that died over forty years (Numbers 14:29–35), so the psalm fits Moses' life. Christian readers such as Luther read it as the law's mirror, showing every person that death is the wage of sin (Romans 5:12; Romans 6:23), so that the gospel can be heard. Many scholars read it as a wisdom meditation on mortality, close to Job 14 and Ecclesiastes.

a: in the light of your face
p: Usually the light of God's face means favor and blessing. Here it is a searchlight on hidden sin.
b: The priestly blessing asks, "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" (Numbers 6:25), and 4:6 prays, "LORD, raise the light of your face above us." In 89:15 the happy people "walk, LORD, by the light from your face." Psalm 90 turns the phrase around: the same light that blesses also exposes what we kept hidden. The Greek reads "our lifetime is in the light of your face," taking a word for "hidden things" as "our age" (both from the root alam).

a: add up to seventy
p: Seventy was a full human life in the ancient Near East. Moses himself, the psalm's named author, lived to 120.
b: Isaiah 23:15 calls seventy years "the lifetime of one king," and David died at about seventy (2 Samuel 5:4). Many lived longer: Moses died at 120 with his strength intact (Deuteronomy 34:7), Joshua at 110. The verse is not a limit set by God but a description of the usual span. The Mishnah's ages of life (Avot 5:21) draw on it: "at seventy, white hair; at eighty, strength," using the psalm's word gevurot, "strength." In Jewish custom an eightieth birthday is sometimes called reaching gevurot.

a: What they boast of is hard work and grief
p: Rohav means pride or boasting. Older versions read a similar word, "the most of them," or guessed "their strength."
b: Even the best of a long life, the things people are proudest of, turn out to be amal (toil, hard labor) and aven (trouble, sometimes wickedness). The Greek and Latin read "and the greater part of them" (to pleion autōn), as if from rubbam, with one vowel and letter different. The KJV has "their strength." The Hebrew as written gives the sharper thought: what we boast of is labor and sorrow.

a: Teach us, then, to count our days
p: The psalm's prayer for wisdom: to see how short life is and live wisely because of it.
b: This is the turning point of the psalm. After the hard truths of 90:3–11, Moses asks not for a longer life but for the skill to number the days given. "Bring in" is a harvest word: the wise heart is the crop gathered from a short life. The Targum reads "Who is fit to teach us to number our days, except the prophet?", meaning Moses himself. Christian writers from Augustine to Luther used the verse to urge readiness for death, and the Anglican burial service of 1662 reads the whole psalm in church before the burial.

a: Change your mind about your servants
p: "Turn back" and "change your mind" are the two verbs Moses used when he begged God to spare Israel after the golden calf.
b: At Sinai Moses prayed, "Turn from your blazing anger. Change your mind about this harm to your people" (Exodus 32:12), and "the LORD changed his mind" (Exodus 32:14). The Hebrew of 90:13 uses the same pair, shuv and nicham. The Song of Moses promises that the LORD will "show his servants pity" (Deuteronomy 32:36), with the same verb again. So the prayer of Moses in the Psalter asks God to do what he did for Moses before. "How long?" is the cry of the laments (6:3; 13:1–2; 74:10). On whether God "changes his mind," see the topic page.

a: At daybreak, fill us with your loyal love
p: In the Psalms, morning is when rescue comes. After the night of 90:4–9, the psalm asks for dawn.
b: God helps his city "at the turning of the morning" (46:5); weeping may last the night, but joy comes in the morning (30:5); his mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23). The psalm's whole movement is from night to morning: from the night watch and the grass that withers by evening (90:4–6) to the prayer that God's loyal love would satisfy his people at daybreak, so that their remaining days are glad ones.

a: Let the kindness of the Lord our God be on us.
p: No'am is pleasantness, beauty, delight. The last verse asks that God's own loveliness rest on his people and their work.
b: No'am is what the singer of 27:4 longs to see: "how lovely the LORD is." The Greek has "the brightness of the Lord," the Targum "the pleasantness of the Garden of Eden." In Jewish prayer this verse, called Vihi No'am, is joined to Psalm 91 and said at the close of the Sabbath on Saturday night, as the work week begins. The prayer is fitting: a psalm that began with the shortness of human life ends by asking God to make the work of human hands last.

a: the hiding place of the Most High
p: Two verses use four names: the Most High, the Almighty, the LORD and my God.
b: Elyon, "Most High," is the title of the God whom Melchizedek served (Genesis 14:18–20). Shaddai, "the Almighty," is the name of the God of the patriarchs (Exodus 6:3). Then the singer names YHWH, the LORD, and calls him Elohai, "my God." The two old, lofty titles are claimed under the personal name and the personal pronoun. "Hiding place" (seter) is the same word as in 27:5, 31:20 and 32:7. Rashi reads it as shelter "in the covert of the wings of the Shekhinah," God's dwelling presence.
orig: בְּסֵתֶר עֶלְיוֹן ... בְּצֵל שַׁדַּי (beseter elyon ... betsel shaddai)

a: will spend the night in the shadow of the Almighty
p: Lun is to lodge for the night, as a traveler does. The "shadow" is shade from the sun and cover from danger.
b: The verb yitlonan is used of a guest who stays overnight (Genesis 19:2; Judges 19:4). The psalm promises safe lodging through the night, when the terrors of 91:5–6 roam. "Shadow" in the Psalms often belongs with God's wings (17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 63:7). The Targum reads "in the shadow of the clouds of the glory of Shaddai," thinking of the cloud that covered Israel in the wilderness.

a: This is what I say to the LORD:
p: The voices change: "I" (91:2), "you" (91:3–13), "I" again (91:9), then God (91:14–16). Readers explain it differently.
b: A temple liturgy. Many scholars, after Mowinckel, think a worshiper makes a confession of trust (91:2, 9a), a priest or Levite answers with promises (91:3–13), and a closing oracle gives God's own word (91:14–16). A teacher and pupil. Others hear a wisdom teacher instructing a student. The Targum makes it a dialogue: David speaks to his son Solomon, Solomon answers (91:9), and "the Lord of the world" replies. Christian readers often hear the Father speaking of Christ, as in the temptation story (Matthew 4:6). The Greek has "he will say to the Lord," which smooths the change.

a: My shelter and my fortress
p: Machseh is a place to run to for cover. Metsudah is a mountain stronghold, like the ones David hid in.
b: Metsudah is a rocky stronghold, such as the strongholds of En-gedi and Adullam where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:4; 1 Samuel 24:22). David uses it of God in 18:2. Machseh, from the verb "take shelter," is what God is in 46:1 and 62:7. The psalm gathers words of safety: hiding place, shadow, shelter, fortress, wings, shield, wall, home. The same "shelter" returns in 91:9, binding the psalm together.

a: the bird-catcher's trap
p: Birds were caught with nets, clap-traps and snares. The picture is of a danger you do not see until it springs.
b: Egyptian tomb paintings show fowlers pulling clap-nets over flocks in the marshes, and Amos asks whether a bird falls into a trap when no bait is set (Amos 3:5). Psalm 124:7 thanks God that "The trap snapped, / and we got loose." Proverbs 7:23 compares a young man led into adultery to a bird rushing into a snare. In the Psalms the trap usually stands for a plot laid by enemies (140:5; 141:9).

a: With his long feathers he will cover you over
p: A mother bird covering her young, or the cherubim's wings over the ark? Both pictures have been seen here.
b: The image is tender: God as a bird spreading her wings over her chicks, as the eagle of Deuteronomy 32:11 spreads its wings over its young. Boaz blesses Ruth as one "under whose wings you have come for refuge" (Ruth 2:12), and Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem's children "the way a bird gathers her young under her wings" (Matthew 23:37). Some scholars also hear the temple, where the cherubim's wings covered the ark (1 Kings 8:6–7), so that shelter "under his wings" means shelter in the sanctuary. Evrah is a long wing feather, a pinion.

a: A shield and a wall
p: Tsinnah is a large body shield. Socherah appears only here; it may mean a rampart around a camp or a small shield.
b: Most of the psalm's protection words are about places to hide. These two are about armor and defenses. The tsinnah was the big shield carried in front of a warrior (1 Samuel 17:7). Socherah, found nowhere else, comes from a root meaning "to go around," so it may be a wall or rampart surrounding a person, or a round shield. The Greek has "his truth will surround you with a shield." God's faithfulness, his reliability in keeping his word, is the armor.

a: what terrifies at night
p: Ancient people feared demons of night and noon. The psalm names terror, arrow, plague and scourge, perhaps as figures.
b: In Canaan and Mesopotamia, disease and sudden death were often pictured as demons or gods. Resheph, a Canaanite plague god, was called "lord of the arrow," and Deber ("plague") and Resheph walk before God in Habakkuk 3:5. The Babylonians feared Lamashtu and the night demons later called lilu and lilitu (compare Isaiah 34:14). Psalm 91 may use these names as figures of speech, the way English speaks of a plague "stalking" a city. The verdict: the language draws on that shared world, but the psalm gives these powers no rule of their own. The Targum and the Greek made them demons outright (see 91:6).
r: Habakkuk 3:5; Deuteronomy 32:24; Isaiah 34:14; Job 5:7; Song of Songs 3:8

a: Though a thousand drop at your side
p: Some read Psalm 91 as a guarantee that believers will never be harmed. The rest of the Bible complicates that.
b: Psalm 91 has been carried into battle, sewn into uniforms and prayed in epidemics, and is often called "the soldier's psalm." Its promises are sweeping: no harm, no plague (91:10). Some readers take them as a literal guarantee for those who trust. Most Jewish and Christian teachers read them as the language of trust, true of God's care but not a promise that nothing bad will happen: Job was blameless and suffered, the righteous of Psalm 44 were killed all day long, and Jesus refused to use 91:11–12 to test God (Matthew 4:7). Calvin taught that the promises hold even when believers suffer, because nothing touches them outside God's care.

a: For you, LORD, are my shelter!
p: The Hebrew breaks out in the first person in the middle of promises to "you." Many translations smooth it over.
b: Word for word, 91:9 reads "For you, LORD, my shelter; the Most High you have made your home." The first half is a cry of trust, like 91:2; the second goes back to addressing the listener. Many English versions join the two into one sentence about the listener ("Because you have made the LORD your refuge"), adding words the Hebrew does not have. The Greek keeps the break: "For you, Lord, are my hope." The Plain keeps it too, because the change of voice is part of how the psalm works (see 91:2).

a: no stroke of disease will come near your tent
p: Nega is a blow or a stroke, often a disease that strikes. It is the word for the skin disease of Leviticus.
b: Nega is "touch," a blow that lands on someone. It names the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 11:1) and the skin disease of Leviticus 13–14. "Your tent" is your home, the place where you live. The line recalls the Passover night, when the destroyer passed over the houses marked with blood (Exodus 12:13, 23). The Targum adds "no plague or demon shall come near your tents."

a: he will give his angels orders about you
p: The verse is a main text for the belief that God gives angels to guard people.
b: Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that each believer has a guardian angel from birth; the Catholic Catechism cites the Psalms and Matthew 18:10 (Catechism 336). Many Protestants affirm that angels serve God's people (Hebrews 1:14) but do not teach that each person has one assigned angel, since Scripture does not say so directly. Jewish tradition knows protecting angels too; the Talmud says two angels accompany a person home on Sabbath eve (Shabbat 119b). The psalm itself speaks of angels guarding "you" on every road, without saying how many.
r: Matthew 18:10; Hebrews 1:14; Genesis 24:7; Exodus 23:20; Psalm 34:7; Acts 12:15

a: Their hands will hold you up
p: In the temptation story the devil quotes 91:11–12 to Jesus on the temple's pinnacle. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy.
b: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down," says the devil, "for it is written that he will give his angels orders concerning you" (Matthew 4:6, a fresh rendering; compare Luke 4:9–11). Matthew leaves out "to guard you on every road you take"; Luke keeps "to guard you." Jesus answers, "Do not put the Lord your God to the test" (Deuteronomy 6:16), the verse that recalls the testing at Massah, the place Psalm 95:8 names. The psalm promises protection to one who trusts; using it to force God's hand is the opposite of trust. Many later readers have noticed that the quotation stops just before 91:13, where the serpent is trampled.

a: Lion and cobra you will walk upon
p: Lion and snake stand for every danger, wild and hidden. Christians linked the line to Genesis 3:15 and Luke 10:19.
b: Lions and snakes were the deadliest animals a traveler met. Tannin can be a large snake (Exodus 7:9) or a sea monster (74:13), so the Greek has "dragon." Jesus tells his disciples, "I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions" (Luke 10:19, a fresh rendering), and Paul promises that God will crush Satan under his people's feet (Romans 16:20). Christian art, for example the mosaic in the Archbishop's Chapel at Ravenna (about AD 500), shows Christ as a soldier treading on a lion and a snake, taken from the Latin of this verse.
orig: שַׁחַל וָפֶתֶן ... כְּפִיר וְתַנִּין (shachal vafeten ... kefir vetannin)

a: Because he has fastened his heart on me
p: Chashaq is a strong word for attachment. Deuteronomy uses it for God setting his love on Israel.
b: Chashaq means to be bound to someone in desire. Shechem's heart "clung" to Dinah (Genesis 34:8), and the LORD "set his heart" on Israel's ancestors (Deuteronomy 7:7; 10:15). Here the love runs the other way, from the person to God, and God answers with seven promises in three verses: I will get him out, set him high, answer, be with him, pull him out, honor him, fill him with long life and show him my saving help. "Knows my name" means a person in a real relationship with God, who calls on him by name (9:10).

a: I will fill him with long life
p: The Talmud calls Psalm 91 a "song against afflictions." It is said at bedtime, at Sabbath's end and at funerals.
b: The Talmud names Psalm 91 among the "songs of afflictions" (shir shel pega'im), recited for protection (Bavli Shevuot 15b). It is part of the prayers at bedtime, is said on Saturday night with 90:17, and in many communities is recited at a funeral while walking with the body to the grave, sometimes with seven pauses. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, a scroll of songs against demons (11Q11) ends with a form of Psalm 91, which shows that it was already used this way before the time of Jesus.

a: A song for the Sabbath day
p: The only psalm the Hebrew assigns to a day. The Levites sang it on the Sabbath, and Jews still sing it on Friday night.
b: The Mishnah lists the psalm the Levites sang at the temple each day: 24, 48, 82, 94, 81, 93, and on the Sabbath, Psalm 92, "a song for the time to come, for the day that will be all Sabbath and rest" (Tamid 7:4). The Greek titles of Psalms 24, 48, 94 and 93 also name these days, so the custom is older than the Mishnah. Nothing in the psalm mentions the Sabbath, which has puzzled readers. The Targum says the first man, Adam, sang it on the first Sabbath. In the synagogue it ends the Friday evening welcome of the Sabbath (Kabbalat Shabbat) and is read again on Sabbath morning.

a: It is a good thing to thank the LORD
p: Readers have found the Sabbath link in rest from work, in praise of creation, and in the end-time Sabbath.
b: Rest and praise. Radak says the Sabbath is better than other days for praising the Name, because a person is free of the world's business. Creation. The psalm praises "the work of your hands" (92:4), the work God rested from on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2). The world to come. The Mishnah and Rashi read it as a song for the coming age that will be "all Sabbath," when the wicked are gone (92:7, 9) and the righteous flourish. Christian readers have sung it on the Lord's Day, and Hebrews 4:9 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for God's people.

a: on the ten-string and on the harp
p: Three instruments: a ten-stringed instrument, the larger harp (nevel) and the lyre (kinnor).
b: The kinnor was a hand-held lyre with a wooden frame, David's instrument (1 Samuel 16:23). The nevel was probably a larger lyre or harp with a sound box; "ten-string" (asor) may be a separate instrument or describe the nevel itself, as in 33:2 and 144:9. Higgayon, "low hum," comes from the verb for murmuring; it appears as a musical mark in 9:16. Rashi reports a rabbinic debate over whether kinnor and nevel differ only in the number of strings.

a: A stupid person does not know it
p: Ba'ar is someone as dull as an animal; kesil is the stubborn fool of Proverbs. Psalm 94:8 uses the same pair.
b: Ba'ar comes from be'ir, "livestock": the person who lives like an animal and does not think (73:22, "I was a dumb animal with you"; 49:10). Kesil is Proverbs' word for a fool who will not learn. What they cannot see is God's deep plan (92:5): that the wicked flourishing like grass are doomed. The same pair addresses the wicked in 94:8, one of many links between neighboring psalms in Book IV.

a: the wicked may spring up like grass
p: The psalm faces the question of Psalms 37 and 73: why do the wicked prosper? Its answer is that grass does not last.
b: Psalm 92 sets two plants side by side: the wicked are grass that springs up fast and is gone (compare 90:5–6; 37:2), and the righteous are palms and cedars that grow slowly and bear fruit in old age (92:12–14). The answer is not that the wicked never thrive, but that their thriving is short. Scholars note that Psalm 92 answers Psalm 73's crisis with Psalm 1's picture of the tree. Readers who find this too neat point to Job and Ecclesiastes, and to the fact that the psalm itself prays and hopes rather than describes what it already sees.

a: For look at your enemies, LORD!
p: This three-part line closely matches a line in the Baal poems from Ugarit, written centuries earlier.
b: In the Baal Cycle from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), the craftsman god says to Baal: "Look, your enemy, O Baal, look, your enemy you will strike down; look, you will destroy your foes." Psalm 92:9 has the same build: "look ... your enemies," repeated, then the enemies destroyed. Psalm 93:3 has the same stepping pattern. The verdict: a real link of poetic form, inherited by Hebrew poets from the shared Canaanite tradition. The meaning is changed: in Ugarit Baal must fight to become king; in Psalm 92 the LORD is already on high forever (92:8).

a: my horn like a wild ox's
t: The horn of the wild ox
p: A horn is a picture of strength. The re'em was the wild ox, the aurochs; the KJV's "unicorn" comes from the Greek.
b: To raise someone's horn is to make them strong and victorious, like a bull tossing its head (75:4–5; 89:17; 1 Samuel 2:1; Luke 1:69). The re'em was the aurochs, the huge wild ox of the ancient Near East, now extinct, hunted by Assyrian kings (22:21; 29:6; Job 39:9–10). The Greek translators rendered it monokerōs, "one-horn," perhaps because Assyrian carvings show the animal in profile with one horn visible. Through the Latin unicornis this became the KJV's "unicorn." No mythical animal is meant.

a: The righteous will sprout like the date palm
p: The tall date palm and the long-lived cedar were the most stately trees Israel knew. Both were carved in the temple.
b: The date palm (tamar) grows tall, bears fruit for generations, and stays green in the desert. The cedar of Lebanon was the great timber tree of kings. Solomon's temple was paneled with cedar and carved with palm trees and cherubim (1 Kings 6:15–18, 29), and Ezekiel's temple has palms on its walls and gates (Ezekiel 40:16; Ezekiel 41:18). So when the righteous are "planted in the LORD's house" (92:13), they become the living version of the temple's carvings, like the olive tree in God's house in 52:8. The picture recalls Psalm 1:3, the tree by channels of water.
r: 1 Kings 6:15–18; 1 Kings 6:29; Ezekiel 40:16; Ezekiel 41:18; Psalm 1:3; 52:8; Jeremiah 17:7–8; Revelation 22:2

a: In old age they will still yield fruit
p: The psalm promises a long, fruitful life to the righteous, set against the wicked's fast bloom.
b: The trees of 92:12–14 are "plump and green" (deshenim vera'ananim), full of sap. The Targum takes the fruit as children born in old age, like their fathers. The Greek reads "they will grow in a rich old age." Christian and Jewish readers alike have found here a word for the elderly: age is not uselessness. Compare Moses, whose vigor did not drain away at 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7), and Caleb, strong at 85 (Joshua 14:10–11).

a: my rock, with no wrong in him
t: The Rock of the Song of Moses
p: The last line borrows from Deuteronomy 32:4, the Song of Moses: the Rock is straight, with no wrong in him.
b: Moses' song says of God: "He is the Rock... He is a God you can trust, with no wrong in him; he is fair and he is straight" (Deuteronomy 32:4). Psalm 92:15 has the same three ideas in nearly the same words: yashar, "straight," tsur, "rock," and "no wrong," with avlatah where Moses has avel. Coming right after the prayer of Moses in Psalm 90, the echo strengthens the Moses voice in the opening of Book IV. The flourishing of the righteous and the end of the wicked are the evidence that God is just.

a: The LORD is King!
t: "The LORD is King" or "has become King"?
p: YHWH malakh opens Psalms 93, 97 and 99 and is the cry of 96:10. Scholars debate whether it means "is" or "has become" King.
b: The verb malakh can describe a state ("is king, reigns") or an event ("has become king"). When Jehu was crowned, the people cried malakh Yehu, "Jehu has become king!" (2 Kings 9:13; compare 2 Samuel 15:10). Sigmund Mowinckel argued that these psalms were sung at a yearly festival where the LORD was hailed as newly enthroned, as a human king was. Others note the word order here, with the name first ("The LORD, he is King"), which stresses who reigns rather than when, and 93:2 says his throne has stood "from the start." The Plain follows the site's rendering of 1 Chronicles 16:31; see the note there on the kingship psalms.

a: He is dressed in majesty.
p: Ge'ut, "majesty," is also the word for the swelling of the sea in 89:9. The LORD wears what the sea boasts of.
b: A king put on robes and a belt to show his power (Isaiah 11:5; Isaiah 22:21). The LORD's robe is ge'ut, "rising, majesty, pride," and his belt is oz, "strength." In 89:9 the same word describes the sea "when it swells," and Jeremiah 12:5 uses it of the Jordan's proud thickets. So the psalm may be playing on the word: the rising that the waters of 93:3 claim for themselves belongs to the LORD, who wears it. God "clothed" in majesty returns in Psalm 104:1–2.

a: Surely the world is set firm; it will not totter.
p: The Greek title gives Psalm 93 to "the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was settled": the day creation was finished.
b: The Greek heads the psalm "For the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was inhabited. A praise of a song, of David." The Mishnah lists it as the Levites' psalm for the sixth day (Tamid 7:4), and the Talmud explains why: on the sixth day God finished his work and reigned over all he had made (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 31a). The firm world of this line, set up and unshaken, is the finished creation. One Qumran scroll, 11QPs-a, opens the psalm with "Praise the LORD!" (see the variant). Jews sing it on Friday evening after Psalm 92, and on Friday mornings as the psalm of the day.

a: The rivers have raised, LORD
p: In the Baal poems from Ugarit, the storm god defeats "Prince Sea, Judge River" and becomes king. Psalm 93 knows the story.
b: In the Baal Cycle, Baal fights Yam (Sea), also called Nahar (River), defeats him, and is proclaimed king; a palace is then built for him. Psalm 93 has the same pieces in the same order: the LORD is king, the world stands firm, the rivers and sea raise their voice, and the LORD's house is holy (93:5). The verdict: a real literary link. But the psalm tells no battle. The waters roar and the LORD is simply greater. Many scholars see the old myth turned into a confession that chaos, whether the sea or the nations (Isaiah 17:12–13), is never a rival to Israel's God.

a: More than the sounds of the vast waters
p: "Many waters" is a fixed phrase for the roaring deep. Ezekiel and Revelation use it for the sound of God's own voice.
b: The phrase mayim rabbim describes the floods that threaten (18:16; 32:6; 144:7) and the chaos God rules (29:3). Ezekiel hears the sound of God's coming glory "like the sound of many waters" (Ezekiel 43:2), and in Revelation the risen Christ's voice is "like the roar of rushing waters" (Revelation 1:15), as is the song of the great crowd: "Hallelujah! For our Lord God, the All-Powerful, rules" (Revelation 19:6). The noise that once rose against God becomes the sound of his reign.

a: Your decrees can be trusted completely.
t: From the sea to the law
p: After the roaring waters comes a quiet line about God's decrees and his holy house. The king rules by his word.
b: Edot, "decrees," are the terms of God's covenant, the testimony kept in the ark (Exodus 25:22, "the ark of the testimony"). Psalm 19 makes the same move from the skies to the law: "The LORD's decree can be trusted" (19:7), using the same verb, ne'emnu. The God who sets the world firm also gives a reliable word. The last line praises his house, the temple: holiness "is fitting" there for all time. Radak notes the hope that the house would never be destroyed again.

a: God who takes vengeance, LORD,
p: The Greek titles it "for the fourth day of the week." The Levites sang it on Wednesdays, and Jews still do.
b: The Greek heads it "A psalm of David, for the fourth day of the week," and the Mishnah lists it as the Levites' psalm for the fourth day (Tamid 7:4). The Talmud gives the reason: on the fourth day God made the sun and the moon, and he will one day punish those who worship them (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 31a). In the synagogue it is still the psalm for Wednesday morning. Psalm 94 follows 93 abruptly: from the King above the sea to a plea that the King act as judge.

a: God who takes vengeance
p: Neqamah in the Bible is not a grudge. It is the punishment a rightful ruler or judge brings on wrongdoers.
b: English "vengeance" sounds like private revenge. The Hebrew neqamah is usually the act of a lawful authority that sets wrongs right, especially when no human court will. The Song of Moses says, "Vengeance belongs to me, and payback" (Deuteronomy 32:35), and Paul quotes it to forbid Christians to take revenge themselves (Romans 12:19). George Mendenhall showed that the word often means the exercise of a sovereign's power to defend his people. Psalm 94 asks God to do exactly that, because those who should judge (94:20) are the ones killing the weak.

a: shine out!
p: Hofia is the verb of God's coming in light, as at Sinai. The psalm asks for an appearance like that.
b: "He beamed out from Mount Paran" (Deuteronomy 33:2) describes the LORD coming to his people at Sinai. "From Zion, beauty made perfect, God shines out" (50:2), and the Shepherd of Israel is asked to "shine out!" (80:1). The verb is a theophany word: it pictures God bursting into view like the sun. In Psalm 94 the light is the light of judgment.

a: Stand tall, Judge of the earth!
p: The title recalls Abraham's bold question over Sodom: will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?
b: Abraham pleaded, "Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25). Psalm 94 assumes the answer is yes and asks God to act on it. "Stand tall" (hinnase, "lift yourself up") is a call for God to rise from his throne as a judge rises to give sentence (7:6; 82:8). The proud are paid gemul, what their deeds have earned, the same word as in 28:4.

a: Widow and foreigner they kill
p: The wicked here are not foreign armies. They are people with power in Israel who crush the weakest.
b: The widow, the foreigner living in the land and the fatherless are the three groups the law protects again and again: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22; compare Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 24:17; Deuteronomy 27:19). The prophets condemn leaders who rob them (Isaiah 1:23; Isaiah 10:1–2; Jeremiah 22:3). Psalm 94 speaks of "your people" and "your inheritance" being crushed (94:5), and of a "throne that brings ruin" making misery into law (94:20). Most scholars read it as a protest against corrupt rulers or judges in Judah. Some hear foreign oppressors as well, since 94:10 speaks of God disciplining nations.
r: Exodus 22:21–24; Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 24:17; Isaiah 1:23; Isaiah 10:1–2; Jeremiah 22:3; James 1:27

a: Yah does not see
p: The Hebrew uses the short form of the divine name, Yah, here and in 94:12. The wicked deny not God, but his attention.
b: "Yah" is the short form of YHWH, heard in "Hallelujah" (see 68:4). The Plain keeps "Yah," as in Exodus 15:2, wherever it stands alone; in "Hallelujah" it is "Praise the LORD!" The oppressors are not atheists in the modern sense. Like the wicked of 10:11 ("He has turned his face away; he never looks") and 73:11, they believe God exists but does not notice or care. The psalm's answer in 94:9–11 is an argument from creation: the one who made eyes and ears sees and hears.

a: Will the one who planted the ear not hear?
p: The maker of ears and eyes cannot be deaf and blind. The psalm argues from what God made to what God is.
b: The questions of 94:9–10 are a teacher's argument. God asked Moses, "Who put a mouth in a human being? ... Isn't it I, the LORD?" (Exodus 4:11). The verb "planted" for the ear is unusual and vivid: the ear is set into the head like a tree into the ground. Philosophers and theologians have used the verse to argue that God must have at least the powers he gives his creatures. Rashi applies it to Israel: can the one who planted the ear fail to hear the cry of his people?

a: no more than a puff of air
p: Paul quotes 94:11 in 1 Corinthians 3:20, but makes it "the thoughts of the wise."
b: Hevel is the "breath" or "vapor" of Ecclesiastes and of 39:5 and 62:9. In the Hebrew it is unclear whether "they" are the people or their thoughts; the Greek says the thoughts are "futile" (mataioi). Paul quotes it from the Greek, adding a word to fit his argument against pride in human wisdom: "The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile" (1 Corinthians 3:20, a fresh rendering). He pairs it with Job 5:13, "He snares the wise in their own cunning."

a: Happy is the one you train, Yah
p: The psalm calls a person happy who is trained by God, even through hard days. The thought runs through Proverbs, Job and Hebrews.
b: Yasar means to train or correct, as a parent does a child. "The LORD's discipline, my son, do not reject" (Proverbs 3:11–12) is quoted in Hebrews 12:5–11, and Eliphaz tells Job, "Think how fortunate a man is when God corrects him!" (Job 5:17). In Psalm 94 the training comes "from your law": instruction that gives calm during evil days while the pit is dug for the wicked. The law here is torah, God's teaching, not only rules.

a: For the LORD will not let go of his people
p: This is the promise Samuel gave Israel, and Paul's answer to whether God has rejected Israel.
b: Samuel told Israel, after they asked for a king, that the LORD would not abandon his people for the sake of his great name (1 Samuel 12:22), using the same verb, natash. Paul asks, "Has God rejected his people?" and answers, "Not at all!" (Romans 11:1–2), echoing this verse in its Greek form. Codex Vaticanus at Psalm 95:4 adds the same words to that psalm, a sign of how linked these neighboring psalms were (see the variant there).

a: the silent place
p: Dumah, "silence," is a name for the world of the dead, where no one praises God. The Greek has "Hades."
b: Psalm 115:17 uses the same word: "The dead do not praise Yah, / nor any who go down to the silent place." In Sheol, the world of the dead, there is no voice or song (6:5; 88:10–12). The Greek and Latin render the line "my soul would soon have lived in Hades" (Latin in inferno). The singer was nearly dead, and God's loyal love held him up when his foot slipped.

a: Can a throne that brings ruin be joined with you
p: The psalm's sharpest charge: rulers who make oppression legal. Can such a throne claim God's partnership?
b: Kisse havvot is "a throne of ruin," and it forms amal, "misery," alei choq, "by decree" or "against the decree." Isaiah condemns the same thing: "Woe to those who decree unjust decrees" (Isaiah 10:1, a fresh rendering). The question expects the answer no: God is not a partner of corrupt power, even when it claims his authority. Christian thinkers on resisting unjust rulers have cited the verse, and the Targum reads "Is it possible that a throne of falsehood should be joined with you?"

a: He has brought their wrongdoing back upon them
p: The psalm ends trusting that wrongdoing recoils on those who do it. God does it, but through their own evil.
b: This is a frequent thought in the Psalms: the wicked fall into the pit they dug (7:15–16; 9:15; 57:6). The verb tsamat, "destroy, make an end of," is repeated (the Plain renders it "destroy" here and in 101:5 and 101:8), like the doubled "God who takes vengeance" of 94:1, framing the psalm. Erich Zenger argued that psalms like this one hand vengeance over to God rather than taking it into one's own hands, so that the victims' rage becomes prayer. On praying such psalms, see the topic page on the curse psalms.

a: Come, let us cry out with joy to the LORD
p: Psalm 95 is the church's daily call to prayer, named from its Latin first words, and opens the Jewish welcome of the Sabbath.
b: Christian use. The Rule of Benedict (chapter 9) has Psalm 95 sung every day at the start of the night office, and the Roman Liturgy of the Hours still begins each day with it as the Invitatory. The Book of Common Prayer of 1662 sets it at Morning Prayer under its Latin name Venite, exultemus Domino. The American prayer book of 1789 replaced the warning of 95:8–11 with 96:9 and 96:13, a change many have debated. Jewish use. The sixteenth-century mystics of Safed began the Friday evening service with Psalms 95–99 and 29, and Lekhu neranenah, "Come, let us sing," still opens Kabbalat Shabbat.

a: the rock that saves us
p: Tsur yish'enu, "the rock of our salvation," names God as a safe height. The phrase echoes the Song of Moses.
b: In the Song of Moses, Israel "treated the Rock who saved him as worthless" (Deuteronomy 32:15). In Psalm 89:26 the king calls God "the rock of my rescue." A rock is a high place out of reach of enemies and floods. Ending the call to praise with "rock" also prepares for the warning of 95:8, since the rock that gave water at Massah and Meribah is part of that story (Exodus 17:6).

a: a great King over all the gods
p: Do the Psalms grant that other gods exist? Readers answer in three ways.
b: The heavenly court. Many scholars read "gods" as heavenly beings under the LORD, the council of 82:1 and 89:6–7, so that the LORD is King over a real host. Empty gods. Others note that 96:5 calls the gods of the peoples "nothing-gods" and read the line as rhetoric: whatever the nations worship, the LORD is above it. Angels or rulers. The Greek and Targum often soften "gods" to angels or judges (compare 97:7). Codex Alexandrinus and a corrector of Sinaiticus read "over all the earth" here, as in 97:9. The Psalms' main concern is not to count gods but to deny that any rival can stand beside the LORD.

a: and the dry ground was shaped by his hands
p: The words recall Genesis 1 and the crossing of the sea, the two great acts of the God who made Israel.
b: Yabbeshet, "dry ground," is a rare form of the word in Genesis 1:9–10 (yabbashah) and Exodus 14:16, where Israel walks through the sea on dry ground. "Shaped" (yatsar) is the potter's verb used for the forming of the man in Genesis 2:7. The God who owns the depths and heights, the sea and the land (95:4–5), is the one who "made us" (95:6). Creation leads to worship, and worship to the covenant (95:7).

a: let us bow low and bend down
p: Three verbs: lie face down, bend low, and kneel. Worship in Israel was done with the body.
b: Hishtachavah is to bow all the way to the ground, the posture of a subject before a king (Genesis 33:3; 1 Kings 1:23). Kara is to bend or crouch. Barakh here means to kneel, the verb behind "bless" (perhaps because blessing was received kneeling). Older English used "worship" for the first; the Plain keeps the bodily sense. Christian liturgies that sing the Venite have often marked these words by kneeling or bowing.

a: the people he pastures, the sheep his hand tends
p: God is the shepherd-king. The psalm turns the familiar phrase around: "people of his pasture, flock of his hand."
b: One would expect "the people of his hand and the flock of his pasture." The psalm crosses the terms, binding people and flock together. Kings in the ancient world called themselves shepherds, and Israel's God is the true one (23:1; 80:1; 100:3; Ezekiel 34:11–16). Jesus calls himself the good shepherd whose sheep hear his voice (John 10:3, 27), which is what 95:7 asks: listen to his voice.

a: Today, if you would only listen to his voice!
p: The Hebrew "if" here is a wish: "if only you would listen!" The line is a hinge into God's own speech.
b: Im with a verb can begin a wish, as in 81:8: "Israel, if only you would listen to me!" The line belongs to the call to worship, and at the same time introduces the warning that follows in God's own voice (95:8–11). The Greek joins it to the next verse: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts," and Hebrews quotes it that way (Hebrews 3:7–8). The word "Today" becomes the heart of Hebrews' argument: as long as it is called "today," the call still stands (Hebrews 3:13; Hebrews 4:7). The Talmud tells that Rabbi Joshua ben Levi asked the Messiah when he would come and was told "Today", which Elijah explained by this verse: today, if you listen (Bavli Sanhedrin 98a).

a: as at Meribah
p: Meribah means "Quarrel" and Massah "Testing." They name the places where thirsty Israel challenged God in the wilderness.
b: At Rephidim, with no water, the people fought with Moses, and "He called the place Massah and Meribah, because the Israelites picked a fight there, and because they put the LORD on trial" (Exodus 17:7). Near the end of the wilderness years, at Kadesh, the same thing happened at "the waters of Meribah" (Numbers 20:13), and Moses and Aaron themselves were barred from the land (Numbers 20:12; compare Psalm 99:8). Deuteronomy warns, "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16), the verse Jesus quotes in Matthew 4:7. Psalm 81:7 also recalls Meribah.

a: when your ancestors put me on trial
p: Nissah and bachan both mean to test or try. Here the people tested God, demanding that he prove himself.
b: Usually God tests his people (Genesis 22:1; Deuteronomy 8:2). In the wilderness the people turned it around and put God on trial, demanding signs although they had seen his work at the sea and the manna. The LORD says of that generation, "Yet they have tested me these ten times and have not listened to my voice" (Numbers 14:22). The rabbis counted the ten tests (Mishnah Avot 5:4). "Not listening to his voice" links Numbers 14 directly to 95:7.
r: Numbers 14:22; Exodus 17:2; Deuteronomy 8:2; Mishnah Avot 5:4; 78:18; 78:41; 1 Corinthians 10:9

a: Forty years I felt disgust at that generation
p: Hebrews quotes these lines from the Greek, but moves "forty years" to the line before and adds "therefore."
b: In the psalm the forty years belong to God's disgust: "Forty years I felt disgust." Hebrews 3:9–10 reads, "where your fathers tested me by trying me and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angry with that generation" (a fresh rendering). Joined that way, the forty years are years of seeing God's works, and the anger follows. Later, Hebrews 3:17 uses the psalm's own order: "With whom was he angry for forty years?" The added "therefore" (dio) also stands in the first hand of the Verona Psalter (Swete's apparatus, R*). It may come from a Greek text Hebrews knew, or the Psalter may have been made to match Hebrews. Lane and Attridge discuss whether Hebrews links the forty years to the time since Jesus' death.

a: I felt disgust
p: Qut means to loathe or feel sick of. The Greek softened it to "I was provoked."
b: Aqut is a strong word: to be sickened by something (Ezekiel 6:9; Ezekiel 20:43; Job 10:1, "My whole being is sick of living"). Rashi takes it as "I quarreled with them." The Greek has prosōchthisa, "I was angry, provoked," and Hebrews follows the Greek. The rest of the line names the cause: a people whose hearts wander and who "do not know my ways," that is, do not live by them.

a: They will never come into my place of rest.
p: The Hebrew oath says only "If they enter my rest...!" leaving the curse unsaid. The rest was the promised land.
b: Hebrew oaths often name the condition and leave out the curse: "If they enter..." means "may such and such happen to me if they enter," so in effect, "they shall never enter." The Greek, and the KJV of Hebrews 4:3 and 4:5, keep the "if." Menuchah, "rest, resting place," is the land: "For up to now you have not come to the resting place and the inheritance the LORD your God is giving you" (Deuteronomy 12:9). It is also the temple, God's own resting place (132:8, 14; 1 Chronicles 28:2). The oath recalls Numbers 14:28–30 and Deuteronomy 1:34–35.
r: Deuteronomy 12:9; Numbers 14:28–30; Deuteronomy 1:34–35; Psalm 132:8; Psalm 132:14; 1 Chronicles 28:2

a: my place of rest
p: Hebrews 3–4 reads "my rest" as God's own Sabbath rest, still open to anyone who hears his voice "today."
b: Hebrews argues in steps. The wilderness generation did not enter because of unbelief (Hebrews 3:16–19). But God's rest is older than the land: it is the rest of the seventh day, when God rested from his works (Hebrews 4:4, quoting Genesis 2:2). Joshua's entry into Canaan cannot have fulfilled it, or God would not still say "Today" through David centuries later (Hebrews 4:7–8). "So then, a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God" (Hebrews 4:9, a fresh rendering). Hebrews credits the psalm to David, as its Greek title does. On how churches apply this to the Sabbath, see the chapter page.

a: sing to the LORD, all the earth
p: Psalm 96 appears almost whole in 1 Chronicles 16:23–33, sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem.
b: Chronicles joins parts of Psalms 105, 96 and 106 into one song (1 Chronicles 16:8–36). The Plain here uses the site's wording of Chronicles wherever the Hebrew is the same. The differences: Chronicles has no "new song" line (96:1a) and no "Sing to the LORD; bless his name" (96:2a); it has "strength and joy" in "his place" for "strength and beauty" in "his sanctuary" (96:6); "come into his presence" for "come into his courts" (96:8); it has no "He will govern the peoples with fairness" (96:10c) and reorders 96:10–11, says "he is coming" once, and stops before the last two lines of 96:13. Most scholars think Chronicles drew on the psalm; some think both drew on an older song.

a: Sing a new song to the LORD
p: A new song celebrates a new act of God. In Revelation the new song is sung to the Lamb.
b: "A new song" appears in 33:3, 40:3, 98:1, 144:9 and 149:1, and in Isaiah 42:10, which is very close to this psalm. It answers a fresh rescue or victory. The Greek title links Psalm 96 to the rebuilding of the temple "after the captivity," and many scholars hear the voice of Isaiah 40–55 throughout: good news, idols as nothing, the nations called, the coming of the LORD. In Revelation, the elders "sang a new song" to the Lamb (Revelation 5:9), and the 144,000 sing one before the throne (Revelation 14:3).

a: Bring the good news of his saving help each day
p: Bisser is to announce good news, the verb of Isaiah's herald. In Greek it is euangelizō, the root of "gospel."
b: Isaiah hears a herald on the mountains "who brings good news, who announces peace" and says to Zion, "Your God is King!" (Isaiah 52:7), the same message as 96:10. The Greek here is euangelizesthe, "announce the good news," and the New Testament takes up the word for the message about Jesus (Romans 10:15 quotes Isaiah 52:7). In the psalm the good news is yeshu'ah, saving help, told day after day.

a: Every god of the peoples is a nothing-god
p: The Hebrew calls the gods elilim, "nothings." The Greek has "demons," and Paul seems to know that reading.
b: On elilim, see the note at 1 Chronicles 16:26. Where the Hebrew calls the nations' gods empty, the Greek translators wrote daimonia, "demons," as in Deuteronomy 32:17. Paul combines both ideas: an idol is nothing, yet "what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20, a fresh rendering; compare 1 Corinthians 8:4). Many early Christian writers took the Greek of this verse as proof that the pagan gods were demons. The Hebrew contrast is simpler: the gods are nothing, but the LORD made the heavens.

a: Carry a gift and come into his courts
p: Minchah is the word for the grain offering, and also for the tribute a subject paid a king. Here the nations bring it.
b: In the laws of sacrifice minchah is the grain offering (Leviticus 2). Outside them it is a gift of homage, the tribute that subject kings sent to their overlord (2 Samuel 8:2; 1 Kings 4:21). The psalm asks the "clans of the peoples" (96:7) to come into the temple courts with tribute, as subjects of the King. The prophets hope for the same: the nations bringing gifts to Zion (Isaiah 60:5–7; Zephaniah 3:10; Malachi 1:11). Chronicles has "come into his presence" instead of "his courts" (see 1 Chronicles 16:29).
r: Leviticus 2:1; 2 Samuel 8:2; 1 Kings 4:21; Isaiah 60:5–7; Malachi 1:11; 1 Chronicles 16:29

a: He will govern the peoples with fairness.
p: The same words as 9:8, and close to 98:9. The King's rule over the nations is a rule of justice.
b: "He will govern the nations with fairness" (9:8) uses the same verb, din, and the same word for fairness, mesharim, "straightness." Psalm 98:9 ends with it too. For people under foreign empires, the claim that the LORD would judge all peoples fairly was both comfort and challenge: the nations' gods and kings are not the last word. The world "set firm" (as in 93:1) is the stage for that just rule.

a: let the sea thunder with everything that fills it
p: Heavens, earth, sea, fields and forests all rejoice. The whole created world welcomes its coming King.
b: The sea, which rose against God in 93:3, now thunders in praise. Isaiah 44:23 and 55:12 also call mountains and trees to sing and clap. Paul speaks of creation itself waiting "with eager longing" to be set free (Romans 8:19–22). The picture is not of nature worship but of a world that belongs to its maker and is glad when he comes to set it right. The Greek reads "let the sea be shaken."

a: because he is coming to judge the earth
p: Jewish and Christian readers both hear a future coming of God to judge. They differ over how it happens.
b: The repeated "he is coming" makes the judgment near and personal. Jewish tradition hears the coming kingdom of God, when the Presence returns to Zion and the world is set right. Christian readers hear the second coming of Christ, whom God appointed as judge: Paul at Athens said God "has set a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness" (Acts 17:31, a fresh rendering), language close to this verse. Many scholars also hear the yearly festival celebration of God's kingship (see 93:1). The note at 1 Chronicles 16:33 compares the endings.

a: may the many islands be glad
p: Iyyim are coasts and islands across the sea, the far edge of the known world. Isaiah 40–55 uses the word often.
b: To a Judean, the islands and coastlands of the Mediterranean were the most distant places (Genesis 10:5; Jeremiah 2:10). Isaiah has the islands wait for God's teaching and sing his praise (Isaiah 42:4; Isaiah 42:10–12; Isaiah 49:1; Isaiah 51:5). Psalm 97 begins where Psalm 96 left off: the whole earth, to its farthest shores, is glad that the LORD is King.
r: Isaiah 42:4; Isaiah 42:10–12; Isaiah 49:1; Isaiah 51:5; Genesis 10:5; Zephaniah 2:11

a: Cloud and dense darkness are all around him
p: Cloud, darkness, fire, lightning, the earth trembling: the psalm describes the King's coming as Sinai was described.
b: At Sinai there was "thunder and flashes of lightning, a heavy cloud on the mountain" (Exodus 19:16), and "Moses went up close to the deep darkness where God was" (Exodus 20:21), the same word, arafel, as here. Solomon said at the temple's dedication that the LORD "will live in the thick dark cloud" (1 Kings 8:12). The second line repeats 89:14, "Your throne rests on righteousness and justice": the mystery around God hides no unfairness. See the note at 89:14 on the throne's foundation.

a: Like wax, the mountains melt away in the LORD's presence
p: The prophets describe God's coming the same way: mountains melt, valleys split.
b: Micah 1:4 says the mountains melt under him "like wax before the fire," and Psalm 68:2 prays that the wicked perish, "As wax melts in front of fire" (Psalm 68:2). Judges 5:4–5 and Habakkuk 3:6 also shake the mountains when the LORD marches out. "The Lord of all the earth" (adon kol ha'arets) is the title used at the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 3:11, 13) and in Zechariah 4:14.
r: Micah 1:3–4; Psalm 68:2; Judges 5:4–5; Habakkuk 3:6; Joshua 3:11; Zechariah 4:14; Nahum 1:5

a: a carved image
p: Pesel is an image carved from wood or stone. Worshipers who boast in such things will be put to shame.
b: The second commandment forbids making a pesel (Exodus 20:4). Isaiah mocks those who carve gods from the same log they cook with, and says they will be put to shame (Isaiah 42:17; Isaiah 44:9–20). The psalm joins the carved images with elilim, the "nothing-gods" of 96:5. Shame in the Bible is not only a feeling but public failure: trusting something that does not save.

a: the daughters of Judah
p: "Daughters" of a city are its villages, or its women singing at a victory. The line repeats 48:11.
b: In Hebrew a capital's "daughters" are the towns around it (Numbers 21:25; Joshua 15:45). Women also led the songs of victory (Exodus 15:20–21; 1 Samuel 18:6), so the "daughters of Judah" may be singers. Psalm 48:11 has almost the same line: "Mount Zion rejoices; / the daughters of Judah are glad / because of your rulings." The "rulings" (mishpatim) are God's acts of judgment that set things right.

a: You who love the LORD, hate what is evil.
p: After the thunder of God's coming, the psalm turns to its hearers: love for God shows itself in rejecting evil.
b: The prophets say the same: "Hate evil and love good" (Amos 5:15), and Proverbs 8:13 says the fear of the LORD is to hate evil. Paul writes, "Hate what is evil; hold on to what is good" (Romans 12:9, a fresh rendering). The promise follows: God guards the lives of his chasidim, his "loyal ones," the people bound to him in hesed. Some scholars change a few letters to read "The LORD loves those who hate evil," but no manuscript has it.

a: A psalm.
p: Psalm 98 is the only psalm from 93 to 99 with a title in the Hebrew, and its title is simply "A psalm."
b: The Greek and Latin read "A psalm of David." The Targum calls it "A song of prophecy," reading it as a song about the future. Psalm 98 is a twin of Psalm 96: both begin with "Sing a new song to the LORD" and end with the LORD "coming to judge the earth" (96:13; 98:9). Where 96 calls the nations to worship, 98 celebrates a victory already won and seen by the whole world.

a: His right hand brought him victory,
p: Hoshi'ah lo, "saved for him," is the divine warrior winning by his own strength, with no one to help.
b: At the sea Israel sang, "Your right hand, O LORD, smashes the enemy" (Exodus 15:6). Isaiah uses the very phrase of this verse: when no one would step in, "my own arm brought me victory" (Isaiah 59:16; Isaiah 63:5). The "holy arm" is bared before the nations in Isaiah 52:10, in words close to 98:3. The victory is not named. Scholars suggest the exodus, the return from Babylon, or a festival celebration of God's kingship; the psalm leaves it open so it can be sung for every rescue.
r: Exodus 15:6; Exodus 15:12; Isaiah 59:16; Isaiah 63:5; Isaiah 52:10; Luke 1:51

a: He has called to mind his loyal love
p: Mary's Magnificat echoes this verse: God helped Israel, "remembering mercy." Isaiah 52:10 shares its last line.
b: Mary sings that God "has helped Israel his servant, remembering mercy, just as he spoke to our fathers" (Luke 1:54–55, a fresh rendering), and that "he has done mighty deeds with his arm" (Luke 1:51, a fresh rendering), both from Psalm 98. Isaiah 52:10 has nearly the same words as the end of 98:3: all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God. The order matters: God remembers his loyal love to Israel, and the whole earth sees the result.

a: Raise a shout to the LORD, all the earth!
p: Heri'u is the battle cry and the shout of acclaim when a king is crowned. All the earth is told to raise it.
b: Teru'ah is the shout of an army going into battle (Joshua 6:5) and the cry when Israel acclaimed its first king: "all the people raised a shout. 'Long live the king!' they said" (1 Samuel 10:24). Balaam heard "a king's battle cry" ringing out among Israel (Numbers 23:21). In Psalms 47, 95, 98 and 100 the same shout honors the LORD as King. The verbs that follow, "burst into song" and "cry out with joy," are Isaiah's (Isaiah 44:23; Isaiah 49:13; Isaiah 52:9).

a: To the sound of trumpets and ram's horn
p: The silver trumpets were blown by priests; the shofar was a ram's horn. Both sound before the King here.
b: The chatsotsrot were long straight trumpets of hammered silver that the priests blew at festivals and over the sacrifices (Numbers 10:2, 10; 1 Chronicles 15:24). The shofar was a ram's horn, used for signals and for the coronation of kings (1 Kings 1:39; 2 Kings 9:13). The Mishnah says that on the New Year in the temple a shofar was blown with two trumpets beside it (Rosh Hashanah 3:3). For that reason many have tied the kingship psalms to the autumn festival of the New Year, when Jews still proclaim God as King with the shofar.

a: Let the rivers clap palm to palm
p: In 93:3 the rivers raised their voices against God. Now they clap for him like a crowd at a coronation.
b: Clapping was part of acclaiming a king (2 Kings 11:12; Psalm 47:1). Isaiah 55:12 says the trees of the field will clap their hands. The rivers, which in Canaanite myth were God's enemies and in 93:3 roared their pounding, have become applauding subjects. Nothing in creation is left outside the celebration.

a: before the LORD, for he is coming to judge the earth.
p: Isaac Watts' hymn "Joy to the World" (1719) is a paraphrase of the second half of this psalm.
b: Watts set the psalms "in the language of the New Testament," and his version of Psalm 98 begins "Joy to the world! The Lord is come." Watts meant Christ's reign over the world; the hymn became a Christmas carol in America in the 1800s, with a tune adapted by Lowell Mason. Its third verse, about the curse of thorns being undone, adds Genesis 3:17–18 to the psalm's joy. In Anglican Evening Prayer the psalm, under its Latin name Cantate Domino, may be sung in place of the Magnificat.

a: Let the peoples tremble.
p: Ragaz is to shake, with fear or with anger. The Greek reads "let the peoples be angry."
b: Yirgezu can mean to quake in awe or to tremble in anger (Proverbs 29:9). Most translations take it as awe before the enthroned King, as the parallel "let the earth shake" suggests. The Greek and Latin have "let the peoples be angry" (orgizesthōsan, irascantur), the nations raging uselessly against God's rule, as in Psalm 2:1.

a: He sits on the cherubim as his throne
p: The ark in the inner room of the temple had two golden cherubim. The LORD was pictured as invisibly seated above them.
b: The ark was "the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies, who sits on the cherubim as his throne" (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2). God told Moses, "From above the lid, from between the two cherubim on the ark of the testimony, I will tell you everything I command you" (Exodus 25:22). Royal thrones in Canaan were sometimes flanked by winged sphinxes, which helps explain the picture. The kingship psalms bring the heavenly King down to a place: Zion, the ark, the footstool (99:2, 5).

a: Holy is he!
p: The refrain "Holy is he" sounds three times (99:3, 5, 9), like the seraphim's "Holy, holy, holy" in Isaiah 6:3.
b: The psalm falls into three parts, each ending with God's holiness, the last time in full: "for holy is the LORD our God" (99:9). Many readers link it to Isaiah 6:3, the cry used in the Jewish Kedushah and in the Christian Sanctus, and to the living creatures of Revelation 4:8, who never stop saying "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the All-Powerful." Christian writers from the fathers on have heard the threefold holy as a hint of the Trinity. Jewish readers hear the holiness of the one God, who is near (Zion, 99:2) and yet wholly other.

a: Strong King, lover of justice
p: The Hebrew reads "and the strength of a king loves justice." It may address God, or speak of the human king.
b: Word for word: ve'oz melekh mishpat ahev, "and strength of king justice he loves." Readers take it as a title of God ("Mighty King, lover of justice"), as a statement ("the King's might is that he loves justice"), or as about Israel's earthly king, whose strength is to love justice. Some scholars join it to 99:3: "Holy is he, and mighty, a King who loves justice." The Greek has "and the honor of a king loves judgment." The rest of the verse is clear: God set fairness in place and did justice and right in Jacob.

a: bow low at the footstool for his feet
p: The ark was God's footstool, the place where the invisible King's feet rested. Later the whole temple and earth were.
b: David said he wanted to build "a resting house for the ark of the LORD's covenant, for the footstool of our God's feet" (1 Chronicles 28:2). Psalm 132:7 says, "let us bow low at the footstool for his feet" (Psalm 132:7). Lamentations 2:1 mourns that God forgot his footstool when Jerusalem fell, and Isaiah 66:1 widens it: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool," which Jesus quotes (Matthew 5:35). Ancient kings rested their feet on footstools, and some, like those of Tutankhamun, were carved with conquered enemies.
r: 1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:7; Lamentations 2:1; Isaiah 66:1; Matthew 5:35; Psalm 110:1

a: Moses and Aaron stood among his priests
p: Moses is never called a priest elsewhere, but he did priestly work. Samuel is the great intercessor.
b: Moses offered sacrifice and splashed the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:6–8) and ordained Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 8), so the psalm can count him among the priests. Samuel was a Levite who offered sacrifices (1 Samuel 7:9) and was known for prayer: "I will never sin against the LORD by giving up praying for you" (1 Samuel 12:23). Jeremiah 15:1 names Moses and Samuel together as Israel's great intercessors. The point is that these leaders called on God and he answered, an encouragement to every generation that prays.
r: Exodus 24:6–8; Leviticus 8:1–30; 1 Samuel 7:8–9; 1 Samuel 12:23; Jeremiah 15:1; Exodus 32:11–14

a: In a pillar of cloud he would speak to them
p: God spoke to Moses and to Aaron from the pillar of cloud at the tent of meeting.
b: "As Moses went into the tent, the pillar of cloud came down and stood at the tent's door, and the LORD spoke with Moses" (Exodus 33:9). "The LORD came down in a pillar of cloud" to speak to Aaron and Miriam (Numbers 12:5). Samuel did not live in the wilderness, so the psalm speaks of the three together as a group of God's servants; Rashi says the cloud came to Samuel too. They "kept his decrees, the rule he handed them": the leaders were themselves under the law.

a: and who paid them back for what they did
p: The last line may mean God punished their wrongs, or avenged the wrongs done to them. Readers differ.
b: Noqem al alilotam is "taking vengeance on their deeds." Rashi and most readers take it this way: God forgave Israel for the sake of these leaders, yet he punished the leaders' own misdeeds, as Moses and Aaron were kept out of the land after Meribah (Numbers 20:12). This matches the LORD's own words: "forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin. Yet he will by no means leave guilt unpunished" (Exodus 34:7). Others read it as God avenging what others did to his servants. A few scholars change one letter to read "cleansing them."

a: A psalm for the thank offering.
p: Todah means thanks, and also the thank offering, a sacrifice eaten with friends. The title may mean either.
b: The todah was a peace offering brought to give thanks, with loaves of bread, and eaten the same day (Leviticus 7:12–15). The title may mean the psalm was sung when such an offering was brought, or simply "a psalm of thanks." In the Ashkenazi rite, Mizmor letodah is said in the weekday morning service. It is left out on Sabbaths and festivals, when a private thank offering was not brought, and on the eve of Yom Kippur and during Passover, because the offering's loaves included leavened bread. Other rites differ. The Greek has "a psalm for thanksgiving."

a: Raise a shout to the LORD, all the earth!
p: Psalm 100 became "All People That on Earth Do Dwell," sung to the tune known as the Old Hundredth.
b: William Kethe's metrical version (1561), written among English exiles in Geneva, was set to a tune from the Genevan Psalter by Louis Bourgeois. The tune, called the "Old Hundredth," is also used for the Doxology ("Praise God, from whom all blessings flow"). In the Book of Common Prayer the psalm is the Jubilate Deo, sung at Morning Prayer. The psalm's call to "all the earth" makes it one of the most widely sung texts in the world.

a: Serve the LORD with joy
p: Avad is to work for, to serve, and to worship. Israel was freed from serving Pharaoh in order to serve the LORD.
b: The same verb runs through the exodus: "Let my son go, so he may serve me" (Exodus 4:23), and "you will all serve God on this mountain" (Exodus 3:12). In Egypt it meant forced labor; before the LORD it is worship. Deuteronomy 28:47 warns of what follows when "you did not serve the LORD your God with joy" (Deuteronomy 28:47). The psalm asks for that joyful service.

a: Know this: the LORD, he is God.
p: The confession of Deuteronomy and of Elijah's contest on Carmel, now on the lips of all the earth.
b: Moses told Israel, "So know today, and take it to heart: the LORD is God in the sky above and on the earth below" (Deuteronomy 4:39). At Carmel the people threw themselves face down and cried, "The LORD, he is the God!" (1 Kings 18:39). Psalm 100 asks all the earth (100:1) to know what Israel confessed. The reason given is creation and ownership: he made us, and we belong to him (see the variant on that line).

a: Come through his gates with thanks
p: Psalm 100 is a song for entering the temple: through the gates, into the courts, with thanks and praise.
b: Worshipers coming for a festival or with a thank offering passed through the temple gates into its courtyards. Psalms 15 and 24 ask who may enter; Psalm 118:19–20 says, "Open the gates of righteousness for me." Psalm 100 gives no conditions; it simply invites the nations in. The procession matches the movement of Psalm 95, from "Come" to "Come in, let us bow low" (95:1, 6), and Psalm 100 is often seen as the closing of the group of kingship psalms 93–100.

a: For the LORD is good; his loyal love is forever
p: The refrain of 1 Chronicles 16:34 and Psalm 136, sung at the temple's dedication and its rebuilding.
b: The words appear when the ark comes to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34), when the glory fills Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 5:13), when the exiles lay the new temple's foundation (Ezra 3:11), and in every verse of Psalm 136. Jeremiah 33:11 puts them together with this psalm's title: people "bringing thank offerings" to the LORD's house will sing "Give thanks to the LORD of Armies, for the LORD is good, for his loyal love is forever." See the note at 1 Chronicles 16:34.
r: 1 Chronicles 16:34; 2 Chronicles 5:13; Ezra 3:11; Jeremiah 33:11; Psalm 136:1; Psalm 106:1

a: Of David. A psalm.
p: Psalm 101 is a king's promise to rule with integrity. It has been called a "mirror for princes."
b: Many scholars think it was spoken by a king of Judah, perhaps at his coronation or at a yearly renewal, promising to keep his court clean (101:2–7) and to do justice every morning (101:8). Traditional readers take the title as David's own vow. Luther wrote a long exposition of it in 1534 as a guide for Christian rulers and their officials. Coming after the kingship psalms (93–100), it shows what a human king should be under the King: loyal love and justice, the qualities of God's own rule (99:4). Christian readers such as Augustine heard Christ, the righteous King, speaking.

a: Loyal love and justice: of these I will sing.
p: Hesed and mishpat together sum up good rule. Rashi read the verse as praise for both kindness and judgment.
b: Hesed, loyal love, and mishpat, justice, are the pair the prophets demand: "Keep loyal love and justice" (Hosea 12:6, a fresh rendering; compare Micah 6:8). The king sings of them because he means to practice them. Rashi and the Targum read the verse differently: "If you show me kindness, or if you bring judgment on me, either way I will sing to you," teaching that a person blesses God for the bad as well as the good (compare Bavli Berakhot 60b).

a: When will you come to me?
p: In the middle of the king's vows comes a cry: "When will you come to me?" Readers explain it in several ways.
b: The question breaks the run of promises. A plea for God's presence: the king cannot keep his vows unless God comes to him. A link to David's story: when the ark stalled, David asked, "How can I ever have the LORD's ark come to me?" (2 Samuel 6:9), and some interpreters connect the two. The blameless way: Rashi reads "When will it come to me?" of the straight path itself. Some scholars change the vowels to read "truth will come to me." The Greek keeps the question. On tamim, "blameless," see the note on 15:2.

a: inside my own house
p: "My house" is the palace and the court: family, servants and officials. The king starts reform at home.
b: A king's "house" included his family, his servants and the officials around him (2 Samuel 7:11; 1 Kings 4:1–6). Psalm 101 promises that slanderers, the proud and liars will have no place there (101:5, 7), while the faithful will serve him (101:6). The Targum reads "within my house of study." Bad advisers ruined many kings in Israel's story, such as Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:8–11) and Ahab (1 Kings 21:7).

a: anything worthless
p: Devar beliyya'al is "a thing of worthlessness," anything vile or destructive. The king will not set his eyes on it.
b: Beliyya'al, "worthless," describes evil plans (Deuteronomy 15:9) and the deadly illness of 41:8. To set something "before my eyes" is to aim at it or take it as a goal. The Greek has "a lawless thing"; Jerome's version from the Hebrew keeps Belial, which later became a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). "Those who swerve away" (setim) may be people who fall away from loyalty, or simply crooked deeds.

a: him I will destroy
p: The king vows to silence slanderers and drive out the proud. Readers have taken this as law, as self-discipline, or as Christ's judgment.
b: As a royal vow, 101:5–8 promises what a just king must do: protect people from secret accusers and corrupt officials. Proverbs agrees that a king who listens to lies will have wicked servants (Proverbs 29:12). Many Christian readers, since Augustine and Cassiodorus, have read the verses spiritually, as a person's resolve to drive evil out of the heart, or as Christ's final judgment. Luther insisted that they are about real government: rulers must act against slander and corruption. The psalm does not ask private people to punish anyone.

a: Whoever walks the blameless way
t: Who may live with the king
p: The king's test for his servants matches the temple's test for its guests in Psalms 15 and 24.
b: Psalm 15 asks, "LORD, who is welcome as a guest in your tent?" and answers, "One who walks with a whole heart and does what is right" (Psalm 15:1–2), nearly the same words: 15:2 has holekh tamim, and 101:6 adds derekh, "way," so the Plain has "the blameless way" here. Psalm 24:3–4 asks the same question about the LORD's mountain. Psalm 101 applies to the king's house the standard God applies to his. A king who wants God to "come to" him (101:2) must keep the kind of house God would enter.

a: Morning by morning
p: Kings and judges heard cases in the morning. Absalom rose early to stand by the gate and win the people over.
b: Jeremiah tells the house of David, "Execute justice in the morning" (Jeremiah 21:12, a fresh rendering). Absalom "made a habit of rising early and taking his stand by the road leading to the gate" to meet people coming to the king for judgment (2 Samuel 15:2). Morning was also when God's help comes (46:5; 90:14). The king vows not to let wrong wait. "The city of the LORD" is Jerusalem, as in 48:8.

a: bow low at the footstool for his feet
p: Augustine read the footstool as Christ's flesh, adored before it is eaten in the Eucharist.
b: The Latin read adorate scabellum pedum eius, "adore his footstool." Augustine asked how one may adore the earth, God's footstool (Isaiah 66:1), without sin, and answered that Christ took his flesh from the earth and gave that flesh to be eaten: "no one eats that flesh unless he has first adored it" (Expositions of the Psalms 98.9). Catholic writers have cited the passage for adoring Christ in the Eucharist; Protestant writers have answered that Augustine speaks of adoring Christ, not the bread.
